text: When a JavaScript program starts, what is created first?
explanation: The Global Execution Context (GEC) is created first and pushed onto the call stack. It runs in two phases: memory creation (hoisting) and code execution.

text: What happens in the memory creation phase of an execution context?
options: var variables are set to undefined and function declarations are stored in full
Only let and const are allocated
Callbacks are pushed to the queue
explanation: In the creation phase, var gets undefined, function declarations are stored whole, and let/const are allocated but stay uninitialized (TDZ).
x is hoisted and set to undefined in the memory phase, then assigned 5 during execution.
In the creation phase, the function declaration takes priority over var foo. The assignment 'bar' only happens after the log.
let is hoisted but stays in the Temporal Dead Zone until its declaration line runs.

text: In a browser (normal script, not a module), what is logged?
explanation: Global var becomes a property of the global object (window). Global let/const live in a separate script scope, not on window.
var is function scoped, so x leaks out of the block. let is block scoped, so y doesn't exist outside it, and typeof on an undeclared name returns 'undefined'.
The inner count shadows the outer one only inside the block.
inner has no a of its own, so it looks one level up the scope chain, finds outer's a and stops there.

text: What is logged? (classic interview question on lexical scope)
explanation: Scope is lexical: it depends on where print is written (global), not where it is called. print's outer environment is global, where x is 1.
Assigning to an undeclared variable creates an accidental global in non-strict mode. With 'use strict' it throws a ReferenceError.

text: A lexical environment is made of:
options: Only the variables of the current function
The call stack and the heap
A local environment record plus a reference to the outer (parent) lexical environment
explanation: Each lexical environment holds its own bindings plus a link to its parent. Following those links is the scope chain.

options: A function bundled with references to its outer lexical environment, even after the outer function has returned
A way to close the browser tab
explanation: A closure lets an inner function keep accessing the variables of its outer function after that function has finished.
Each call to counter() creates a new c. a and b have separate closures.

text: What does this print? (most asked closure question)
explanation: var gives one shared i for the whole loop. By the time the callbacks run, the loop has finished and i is 3.

text: Without changing var to let, which change makes the previous loop print 0 1 2?
options: Wrap it in an IIFE: (function (j) { setTimeout(() => console.log(j), 0); })(i);
explanation: The IIFE creates a new scope per iteration, and j captures the current value of i. Using let does the same thing automatically, since it creates a new binding per iteration.
A closure captures a reference to the variable, not a copy of its value at the time it was created.

text: What does this print? (data privacy with closures)
explanation: balance is private. It can only be reached through the closure methods, not as a property.
The closure remembers done, so fn runs only on the first call. Later calls return undefined.

text: Why can closures cause high memory usage?
options: Variables captured by a live closure can't be garbage collected
They copy the whole call stack
explanation: As long as the closure is reachable (for example from an event listener), its captured variables stay in memory.

options: A function passed as an argument to another function, to be called later
A function that returns a number
explanation: Functions are first-class in JS, so they can be passed around. setTimeout, addEventListener and array.map all take callbacks.
greet calls the callback with 'Hi Sam', and the callback uppercases it.
The setTimeout callback goes to the task queue and only runs after the call stack (the synchronous code) is empty, even with a 0ms delay.

text: What does this print? (event loop interview favourite)
explanation: Synchronous code runs first (3). Then the microtask queue runs (promise callback, 2) before the macrotask queue (setTimeout, 1).

options: A callback that throws an error
Deeply nested callbacks that make code hard to read and maintain
explanation: It's also called the pyramid of doom. Promises and async/await flatten it. Interviewers often follow up by asking about inversion of control.
